title: Generative Adversarial Networks for Omics Data: An Overview and Future Directions for Livestock Applications

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《Generative Adversarial Networks for Omics Data: An Overview and Future Directions for Livestock Applications》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Introduction · age70226-sec-0001-p1】Deep generative models are a class of deep learning methods that learn the underlying probability distribution of complex datasets, enabling the generation of realistic synthetic samples (Hayawi et al. 2024; Rivero‐Garcia et al. 2024). These models have been used to address challenges such as limited sample size, missing data, class imbalance, and privacy constraints through data augmentation, imputation, and privacy‐preserving analysis (Yelmen and Jay 2023). Among generative methods, generative adversarial networks (GANs), introduced by Goodfellow et al. (2014), have become a widely used framework for generating synthetic data (Tripathi et al. 2022). In a GAN, a generator network produces candidate samples from random noise, while a discriminator network learns to distinguish real samples from generated ones (Goodfellow et al. 2014). Through this adversarial training process, the two networks are optimized in opposition until the generator produces samples that closely approximate the target data distribution (Gangwal and Lavecchia 2024). This framework has been applied in several non‐biological areas, achieving state‐of‐the‐art results in natural language processing tasks (Thirumagal and Saruladha 2021), computer vision applications (Olaniyi et al. 2022), video synthesis (Aldausari et al. 2023), and audio generation (Donahue et al. 2019).

【Introduction · age70226-sec-0001-p2】Building on their success across these high‐dimensional settings, GANs are increasingly being adopted for omics data, introducing an innovative approach to accelerate research in genomics (Murad et al. 2023; Tripathi et al. 2022). For example, Tamilmani et al. (2022) developed a GAN architecture to synthesize microRNA sequences as biomarkers for cancer detection and showed that augmenting training sets with generated samples can improve classification performance in gene expression analysis. Hazra et al. (2022) applied a GAN‐based approach to generate synthetic cat genomes. The authors reported a mean correlation of 93.7% between real and generated genomes, demonstrating that these models can capture complex biological genomic structure. Similarly, Yelmen et al. (2021) showed that adding GAN‐generated artificial genomes to reference panels increased imputation accuracy by 4.4%, particularly for rare alleles. These examples illustrate that GANs can produce biologically meaningful omics data, laying the groundwork for their application in livestock genomics, where limited data availability and diversity remain key bottlenecks.

sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《Generative Adversarial Networks for Omics Data: An Overview and Future Directions for Livestock Applications》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【Proteomics and Protein Design · age70226-sec-0016-p1】In proteomics and synthetic biology, GANs have been explored as tools for designing novel proteins with specific biochemical properties (Kucera et al. 2022). These approaches aim to generate biologically functional amino acid sequences, potentially reducing the time and cost associated with traditional protein engineering methods. For instance, Gupta and Zou (2019) introduced the feedback GAN (FBGAN), a framework for generating synthetic DNA sequences that encode proteins with desired characteristics such as antimicrobial activity. FBGAN integrates an external evaluator into the GAN architecture to guide the generator toward producing biologically relevant sequences. The evaluator is also a neural network trained on cDNA sequences encoding known non‐antimicrobial and antimicrobial peptides (AMP), learning physicochemical properties associated with antimicrobial activity such as amino acid composition, charge, hydrophobicity, helicity, and sequence motifs. Initially, the generator produces sequences without bias toward any specific functional property. These sequences are then assessed by the evaluator, who calculates the likelihood that each sequence possesses the target characteristics like antimicrobial activity. Sequences exceeding a predefined probability threshold are selected to optimize the generator's performance. This feedback loop refines the generation process by prioritizing sequences that perform well according to the evaluator. The evaluator achieved an accuracy of 0.842, an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.908, a precision of 0.826, a recall value of 0.8608, and the area under the precision‐recall curve of 0.88, demonstrating high predictive performance for identifying AMP‐like sequences. The authors applied this framework to design short antimicrobial peptides (fewer than 50 amino acids), demonstrating that feedback GAN could successfully generate protein candidate sequences with functional potential. Furthermore, FBGAN‐generated sequences shared physicochemical properties such as charge, amino acid composition, hydrophobicity, helicity, and aromaticity with the real data, suggesting that FBGAN successfully learned biologically meaningful AMP‐like sequence patterns for AMP generation.

【Proteomics and Protein Design · age70226-sec-0016-p2】In a related effort, Repecka et al. (2021) developed ProteinGAN, a GAN‐based model trained to generate novel functional proteins using naturally occurring protein sequences as a template dataset. ProteinGAN leverages the sequential patterns and evolutionary signals embedded in protein sequences to synthesize new proteins that resemble naturally occurring ones. The model was tested using malate dehydrogenase as a reference enzyme. Notably, approximately 24% of the ProteinGAN‐generated sequences demonstrated catalytic activity in vitro, indicating that the model could generate proteins with real functional utility. This work represents a significant step toward the use of deep generative models for protein design in synthetic biology, with implications for enzyme engineering, therapeutic development, and industrial biotechnology.

【Introduction · age70226-sec-0001-p2】Building on their success across these high‐dimensional settings, GANs are increasingly being adopted for omics data, introducing an innovative approach to accelerate research in genomics (Murad et al. 2023; Tripathi et al. 2022). For example, Tamilmani et al. (2022) developed a GAN architecture to synthesize microRNA sequences as biomarkers for cancer detection and showed that augmenting training sets with generated samples can improve classification performance in gene expression analysis. Hazra et al. (2022) applied a GAN‐based approach to generate synthetic cat genomes. The authors reported a mean correlation of 93.7% between real and generated genomes, demonstrating that these models can capture complex biological genomic structure. Similarly, Yelmen et al. (2021) showed that adding GAN‐generated artificial genomes to reference panels increased imputation accuracy by 4.4%, particularly for rare alleles. These examples illustrate that GANs can produce biologically meaningful omics data, laying the groundwork for their application in livestock genomics, where limited data availability and diversity remain key bottlenecks.

【Training Instability · age70226-sec-0005-p1】The theoretical objective of GAN training is to reach a Nash Equilibrium, where the discriminator no longer distinguishes between real and generated data (Wolterink et al. 2020). In practice, however, achieving this equilibrium is exceptionally difficult because both networks pursue opposing goals: the generator aims to maximize the probability that the discriminator makes a mistake, while the discriminator aims to maximize its accuracy in distinguishing real from synthetic inputs (Salimans et al. 2016). These opposing forces often lead to unstable training, in which neither network converges to an optimal state, resulting in unrealistic samples or suboptimal solutions (Singh Khanuja and Kaur Khanuja 2021).

sections.title: 图表阅读
sections.text:

【FIGURE 1 · age70226-fig-0001】FIGURE 1 Schematic of a generative adversarial network for synthetic data generation. The generator (blue block) takes random noise from a latent variable z (gray circle) and transforms it into artificial samples. These artificial samples are combined with real data and presented to the discriminator (green rectangle), which outputs a score indicating whether each sample is real or generated. During training, the discriminator learns to distinguish real from artificial data, while the generator is updated to produce increasingly realistic samples until the discriminator can no longer distinguish between synthetic and real samples.

sections.text:
《Generative Adversarial Networks for Omics Data: An Overview and Future Directions for Livestock Applications》：复现时可直接核对的数据、软件或实现线索。

【Software Frameworks and Computational Considerations · age70226-sec-0010-p1】GANs can be implemented using general‐purpose deep learning frameworks, with PyTorch (Paszke et al. 2019) and TensorFlow (Abadi et al. 2016) among the most widely used platforms. These frameworks provide the neural‐network layers, automatic differentiation, optimization algorithms, and hardware acceleration required to construct and train the generator and discriminator. PyTorch provides a flexible framework for defining custom adversarial training loops, whereas TensorFlow and Keras offer both lower‐level model customization and higher‐level interfaces for implementing GAN architectures. Implementations of commonly used GAN variants, including conventional GANs, conditional GANs, and WGAN‐GP, are available within these ecosystems and can be adapted to genomic, transcriptomic, and other omics data structures. In practice, implementation requires specifying the generator and discriminator architectures, loss functions, optimization algorithms, and training hyperparameters, followed by domain‐specific evaluation of the generated data.

【Software Frameworks and Computational Considerations · age70226-sec-0010-p2】The computational resources required for GAN training depend strongly on the dimensionality of the input data, network architecture, batch size, number of training iterations, and extent of hyperparameter tuning. Small tabular omics datasets and relatively simple fully connected architectures may be trained using modest computational resources, whereas high‐dimensional genotype matrices, sequencing data, and more complex convolutional architectures can substantially increase memory and processing requirements. Graphics processing units (GPUs) are commonly used to accelerate the matrix operations involved in deep neural‐network training, although GPU acceleration may provide limited benefit for very small models or datasets. For larger applications, GPU memory can become an important constraint because model parameters, intermediate activations, gradients, and batches of high‐dimensional omics observations must be retained during training. Dimensionality‐reduction approaches, smaller batch sizes, or distributed training across multiple GPUs can be considered when the full dataset or model cannot be efficiently accommodated on a single device.
